status_reasoning: Reviewers identified a major discrepancy between small subthreshold changes (~2 mV or 20% EPSP change) and large suprathreshold effects (>200% increase in spike probability). They state 'it is difficult to reconcile these two findings' and request additional analysis and modeling to explain 'how a 20% change in EPSP peak size can lead to a 200% in spike probability.' The reviewers are not convinced by the authors' evidence ruling out Rin or depolarization changes, noting that average data may mask correlations at the single-cell level.

Reviewers express concern about the reliability of the positive timing (LTP) spiking results, requesting information on 'how many stimulations and how many spikes were recorded' beyond just neuron counts. They note that 'from the figures, e.g. Figure 3C it looks as if there is sometimes only a single spike response in some of the conditions,' suggesting insufficient sampling to reliably estimate low spike probabilities like 0.06 spikes/stim. While the effect is statistically significant at the population level, reviewers question whether the data are robust enough to support the strong claims about sub-to-suprathreshold conversion.

Reviewers identify a 'surprising finding' that the LTD protocol strongly affects subthreshold responses (-32.4%) but 'does not seem to affect spiking output, whereas the LTP paradigm does.' They suggest this may be due to 'large spread and not-normal distribution of baseline spiking' and low cell numbers, noting that 'a decrease in spiking will be hard to detect in cells that barely spike to start with.' Reviewers state the data 'look more like a negative control for the LTP experiments' and request clearer discussion of why experiments may be inconclusive or what the functional relevance of LTD would be if conclusive.

Reviewers challenge the authors' conclusion that changes in Rin or depolarization do not account for spiking changes. They state 'we are not convinced that they make a very convincing case here, because they provide average data, and so it could be that on average the change in Rin is small, but that there is a good correlation between neurons that show a change in firing rate and neurons that show a change in Rin.' Reviewers note that 'the transition from EPSP to spike is nonlinear so the small change in Rin or in depolarisation is just as good as a candidate as a small change in EPSP size.'

Reviewers note that 'no negative control experiments are provided in the text or figures (at least regarding subthreshold activity)' and question whether 'LTP/LTD really dependent on spike pairing' or 'could the effect depend on just depolarization instead?' While the authors present a sham control for spiking, reviewers suggest 'the fact that a sham control did not show anything could be because the STDP protocol does change something, but maybe not what the authors propose,' indicating uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation.

Reviewers state 'the relevance of Figure 4 is unclear' and note 'there are no statistics provided – are the results in Figure 4C significant or not?' They criticize that 'the authors use this figure to essentially describe a general, qualitative phenomenon for which the statistics are not provided, and then they elaborate on it as if it is proven.' Reviewers request either statistical tests to confirm significance, more data, or removal of this section, indicating they do not accept the spatial reorganization claims as currently presented.

Reviewers challenge the strong attribution to STDP specifically, stating 'the authors have pushed very strongly the idea that STDP in particular (as opposed to classical Hebbian LTP/LTD) underlies the phenomenology. Certainly the results are consistent with STDP, but they do not demonstrate definitively that STDP definitively underlies the plasticity.' They note that 'the fact that Pawlak et al use a single spike to induce plasticity does not necessarily mean this is STDP; it just means a single postsynaptic spike is enough' and request that 'alternative possibilities need to be acknowledged and discussed more thoroughly.'

Reviewers do not raise concerns about the computational modeling results showing that presynaptic jitter is necessary to reproduce the broader temporal profile of voltage changes observed in vivo compared to in vitro. The request for additional modeling in point 1 implicitly accepts the existing modeling framework as valid, suggesting reviewers view this computational work as a reasonable explanation for the in vivo/in vitro differences.

Reviewers do not challenge any of the background and contextual claims about sensory coding, STDP theory, or the state of the field. These claims provide the scientific rationale for the study and are implicitly accepted by the reviewers' focus on the experimental results and their interpretation rather than the motivation or background.

Reviewers do not raise concerns about the basic experimental methods, animal subjects, recording locations, or pairing protocols. Their critiques focus on data analysis, interpretation, and the need for additional controls rather than questioning the validity of the core methodological approach.
